article.title: From marketing measurement to commercial decisioning
article.desc: Attribution tells you what happened. Growth needs to know what to do next. Why marketing leaders are moving from measuring the past to deciding the future.
article.intro: Marketing doesn't have a measurement problem. It has a decisioning problem. Most teams have more dashboards than ever, and the next budget move is still a guess.

sections.p: Vanity metrics and last-click attribution are easy to report and hard to act on. When ambition is measured in clicks and impressions, teams optimise what is visible and miss what actually drives growth.

A cost-benefit view asks a different question: what return does each dollar create across channels, brands and time? Answering it means connecting marketing to commercial outcomes, including the effects no single channel report can see.

sections.h: From what happened to what to do next
sections.p: Commercial decisioning turns measurement into forward-looking choices: where to reallocate budget, what to cut and what to scale, with scenarios you can test before you spend.
Audit what your current measurement can and cannot answer. If it only explains the past, it is time to put decisioning on top of it.

article.close: Get a decisioning-readiness check on your current measurement.

persona.t: Jordan is the Growth-Accountable Marketing Leader, the persona anchoring Business-Owner content in all 12 windows. Jordan needs proof that marketing spend drove measurable growth — not vanity metrics.

article.title: Measuring AI-shaped demand your attribution can't see
article.desc: AI assistants now sit between brands and buyers. Why traditional attribution misses that influence, and how to simplify measurement so you can still decide with confidence.
article.intro: AI now sits between you and your buyer. Recommendations, summaries and assistants shape what people consider long before they click, and traditional attribution was never built to see it.

sections.h: Too many signals, too little clarity
sections.p: Marketing leaders already juggle more channels, metrics and models than any team can absorb. Adding AI-driven touchpoints to the pile creates cognitive overload: more data, slower decisions.

Channel-level attribution credits the last trackable step. Influence that happens inside an AI answer, or spills across brands and categories, leaves no clean click to follow, so it is undercounted or ignored.

sections.h: One simpler model, fewer blind spots
sections.p: The answer is not another dashboard. It is a simpler model of what drives demand, one that includes halo effects and AI-influenced demand and learns across brands, so the signal is strong enough to act on.
Start by comparing modelled demand with what your attribution reports. The gap is the influence you are not measuring yet, and the budget you may be putting in the wrong place.

article.close: See ROI Genome reveal the demand your reports miss.

article.title: Plan for volatility: why the annual marketing plan breaks
article.desc: Energy shocks, tariffs and demand swings break static annual plans. How always-on scenario planning helps marketing teams move with the market instead of reacting late.
article.intro: Your plan was right in January. The market didn't agree by March. Energy shocks, tariffs and sudden demand swings now arrive faster than any annual planning cycle can respond.

sections.h: The comfort of the annual plan
sections.p: Annual plans feel safe because they are familiar. That is status quo bias at work: we stick with the process we know, even after the conditions it was built for have changed.
Siloed teams, fixed budgets and once-a-year allocations mean a shock is spotted late and answered later. By the time the plan is revised, the opportunity, or the damage, has already happened.
Scenario planning lets teams model a shock before it lands and re-plan allocation the moment conditions move. Instead of one plan a year, you keep a living plan that moves with the market.

sections.h: Break the mold, one scenario at a time
sections.p: Pick the shock you fear most, model it, and agree in advance what you would change. Teams that plan for volatility don't start from zero when it arrives.

article.close: Book a scenario-planning walkthrough for your next shock.
